I am 60 years old and I have farmed these fields for 45 years. I finished middle school, so I can read the numbers on fertilizer bags and I talk to the seed dealer when he comes to the village, but most of what I know comes from doing it with my own hands and watching what happens on my land and my neighbors' land. I have 10.9 mu in total — 7 mu I keep in wheat and maize rotation, and the other 3.9 mu I plant cotton because cotton brings cash, though it costs more in labor and spray.

The wheat I sowed last October is already in the ground and starting to turn green. I will topdress it with 60 jin of urea per mu in the next week or two, before the jointing stage passes. The dealer told me urea is 46% nitrogen, so I know that gives the crop a strong push when it needs it most. Before sowing last autumn, I hired the rotary tiller for 50 yuan per mu and put down one bag — 100 jin — of 18-22-5 compound fertilizer as the base. I irrigate three times from my well: I already did the winter irrigation, and now I will water at jointing in April and again at grain filling in May. Pumping costs diesel money, so I do not water for nothing, but I will not let the wheat go thirsty at jointing — that is when the yield is made. For chemicals, I sprayed herbicide once right after sowing, and this spring I will spray insecticide twice for aphids and fungicide once because two years ago my cousin lost two hundred jin per mu to rust, and I am not taking that chance. That makes four pesticide applications total for wheat. I expect about 1000 jin per mu.

For summer maize on that same 7 mu, I will plant Zhengdan 958, a hybrid seed. I buy 1.2 bags per mu, about 3 jin of seed. As soon as the wheat combine leaves the field in early June, I will sow the maize directly without plowing — no-tillage. I will put down one bag of 28-6-6 compound fertilizer per mu at sowing time. At the big trumpet stage, around mid-July, I will spread half a bag of urea per mu, about 50 jin. That is the critical time; if the maize does not get enough nitrogen then, the ears will be small and my whole year is ruined. I would rather waste a little fertilizer than have empty ears. I will irrigate twice, at tasseling and grain filling. If July is very dry I might add a third watering, but usually twice is enough. Corn borer is my biggest enemy on maize, so I spray insecticide three times, plus one herbicide spray at the three-leaf stage. Four pesticide applications in total. I expect about 1250 jin per mu.

For cotton on my 3.9 mu, I will plant Guoxinmian, an improved variety. I use 2.5 jin of seed per mu. I will rotary till in late April and lay plastic film to keep the soil warm — about 4 jin of film per mu. Cotton needs heat at the start. Basal fertilizer is one bag of 15-15-15 compound, 100 jin per mu. When the plants start flowering in July, I will topdress with half a bag of urea per mu. Cotton is the most expensive crop for chemicals. I will spray 12 times in total: bollworm comes no matter what, so I spray insecticide every week to ten days during July and August, plus herbicide once, plus growth regulator twice to control height, and fungicide once. I will irrigate three times: at flowering, at boll setting, and at boll opening. I expect around 480 jin of seed cotton per mu. Picking is done by hand, mostly me and my wife, though I may hire a few people for the peak if my sons are not home from the city.

Why these amounts? Last year I used almost exactly this, and I got stable yields. Two years ago I tried cutting back on wheat fertilizer to save money — I used only 80 jin of compound and no topdressing — and my yield dropped to 800 jin per mu. That cost me far more than the fertilizer would have. Lao Wang across the lane did the same on his wheat last year and got 100 jin less per mu than me. I learned my lesson. Fertilizer is expensive: a bag of compound is 130 yuan, urea is around 100 yuan a bag, and with diesel and pesticide my costs add up. But a bad harvest is a disaster, while wasting some fertilizer is just a cost I can absorb. My sons send some money home from their factory jobs, which helps, but I still count every yuan. This plan is what I know works, and at my age I do not gamble with new methods unless I see them work on someone else's field first.
